parts.label: (a)
hints: Hint 1: Think about what would happen if two objects at different temperatures are put in contact - in which direction does thermal energy flow, and when does that flow stop?
parts.proper_answer: There is no net transfer of thermal energy between them.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What Thermal Equilibrium Really Means**
Think of temperature as telling you which way thermal energy wants to flow. If one object is hotter, energy flows from hot to cold. When both are at exactly the same temperature, flow in both directions balances out.

Step 2: **Linking to the Definition**
So being in thermal equilibrium does not mean no energy moves at a microscopic level, it means the net flow is zero. That is why same temperature means thermal equilibrium: $$\text{net } Q = 0$$

parts.label: (b)(i)
hints: Hint 1: Look closely at the shape of the mercury density graph in Fig. 3.1 - what is special about how it falls as temperature rises from 0 to 100 degrees?
parts.proper_answer: The density of mercury varies linearly with temperature, so each value of density corresponds to one unique temperature.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What Makes a Good Thermometer**
A good thermometric property must change steadily and give only one possible temperature for each reading. If the graph goes up and down, one reading could mean two temperatures.

Step 2: **Reading the Mercury Graph**
The mercury line in Fig. 3.1 is a straight line sloping gently down. A straight line means equal temperature rises give equal density falls. Every density value appears only once, so you can convert density to temperature reliably.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
hints: Hint 1: Compare the water graph to the mercury graph - does the water density fall steadily, or does it rise then fall?
Hint 2: Think about what happens near 0 to 4 degrees where the top of the curve is almost flat, and what it means if a horizontal line cuts the curve twice.
parts.proper_answer: The variation of density with temperature for water is non-linear and non-monotonic. The same density occurs at two different temperatures, and in the flat region near the maximum the density hardly changes with temperature.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Spotting the Problem Shape**
Look at the water curve. It starts by rising slightly to a maximum at about 4 degrees, then curves down more and more steeply. It is not a straight line.

Step 2: **Why This Fails as a Thermometer**
Because it goes up then down, a horizontal line can cut it in two places. That means one measured density could mean two different temperatures. Also, near the top the curve is almost flat, so a big change in temperature gives almost no change in density - you could not resolve temperature there.

parts.label: (c)(i)
hints: Hint 1: On the temperature-time graph in Fig. 3.2, look for where heating no longer raises the temperature - what does that flat section tell you about a change of state?
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Reading a Heating Curve**
When you heat a liquid, temperature normally rises. When it starts to boil, all the supplied energy goes into breaking bonds for the change of state, so temperature stays constant.

Step 2: **Finding the Plateau**
In Fig. 3.2 the temperature rises from $25^{\circ}\text{C}$ then becomes flat at $80^{\circ}\text{C}$ from about $t = 21\text{ s}$ onwards. That constant temperature is the boiling point.

parts.label: (c)(ii)
key_concepts: specific heat capacity Q = mc delta theta
hints: Hint 1: Start by finding from Fig. 3.2 how long the warming-up stage lasts and how big the temperature rise is before boiling begins.
Hint 2: Think about where the total supplied energy goes - part warms the liquid and part warms the beaker that is always at the same temperature.
Hint 3: Recall how energy, mass, temperature change and specific heat capacity are linked for both the beaker and the liquid.
Hint 4: Check your units carefully - masses are in g and you need the final answer in $\text{J g}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$, and temperature change in $^{\circ}\text{C}$ equals change in K.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Total Energy Supplied During Warming**
Only the sloping part from $25^{\circ}\text{C}$ to $80^{\circ}\text{C}$ is warming. From the graph this takes $t = 21\text{ s}$. Power means energy per second: $$Q_{total} = Pt$$ $$Q_{total} = 810 \times 21 \approx 1.70 \times 10^{4}\text{ J}$$

Step 2: **Energy That Goes Into the Beaker**
The beaker warms by the same amount, $\Delta\theta = 80 - 25 = 55\text{ K}$. Its energy is: $$Q_{beaker} = m_{beaker}c_{beaker}\Delta\theta$$ $$Q_{beaker} = 42 \times 0.84 \times 55 \approx 1940\text{ J}$$ This energy is not available to the liquid, so it must be subtracted.

Step 3: **Energy Left for the Liquid**
By conservation of energy with insulation from surroundings: $$Q_{liquid} = Q_{total} - Q_{beaker}$$ $$Q_{liquid} \approx 17010 - 1940 \approx 15070\text{ J}$$

Step 4: **Specific Heat Capacity of the Liquid**
Now use the same $Q = mc\Delta\theta$ idea for the liquid and rearrange: $$c = \frac{Q_{liquid}}{m\Delta\theta}$$ $$c = \frac{15070}{120 \times 55} \approx 2.3\text{ J g}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$$

parts.label: (d)
key_concepts: effect of specific heat capacity on heating rate
hints: Hint 1: Think about what a larger specific heat capacity means - for the same power, does the temperature rise faster or slower than in (c)?
Hint 2: Remember water boils at a higher temperature than this liquid - where should your new flat section be, and will it be reached much later within 60 s?
parts.proper_answer: Straight line starting at $25^{\circ}\text{C}$ with about half the gradient of the original, rising to $100^{\circ}\text{C}$ then horizontal.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Slower Warming Because c is Larger**
For the same $P$ and $m$, $\Delta\theta / \Delta t = P/(mc)$. If $c$ is about twice as big, the rate of rise is about half. So start at $25^{\circ}\text{C}$ at $t = 0$ and draw a straight diagonal with roughly half the slope of the Fig. 3.2 line.

Step 2: **Higher Boiling Plateau**
Water boils at $100^{\circ}\text{C}$, not $80^{\circ}\text{C}$. Continue your slower line up to $100^{\circ}\text{C}$ and then draw it horizontal. It will reach $100^{\circ}\text{C}$ much later, near $t = 60\text{ s}$, because it needs about twice the energy per degree and a larger total rise.
